title: Valley Fair Mall stabbing renews focus on hate crimes, extremist rhetoric in Utah
text:
The stabbing of a Muslim man at Valley Fair Mall has renewed questions about the prevalence of hate crimes in Utah and how law enforcement identifies people who
A male employee was hospitalized after being stabbed multiple times at Valley Fair Mall on Monday afternoon, and the suspect was taken into custody, police said.
The stabbing of a Muslim man at Valley Fair Mall has renewed questions about the prevalence of hate crimes in Utah and how law enforcement identifies people who may be moving from extremist rhetoric toward violence. Prosecutors have filed a victim-targeting penalty enhancement in connection with the attack, the term used under Utah law for what is commonly called a hate-crime enhancement. The victim, identified as Sohail, was stabbed about a dozen times.
He has since been released from the hospital and is recovering at home, according to remarks shared during a community town hall Wednesday at the Utah Islamic Center. Man accused of stabbing man at West Valley mall had been granted parole more than onceThe town hall brought together law enforcement officers, elected officials, interfaith leaders and community members to discuss safety and ways to combat hate crimes following the attack.
Speakers included Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill, West Jordan Mayor Dick Burton, police chief Jeremy Robertson, a representative from the FBI, interfaith leaders, and several victims of Islamophobia. Sohail briefly joined the gathering by video. Despite the severity of his injuries, he said he did not hold a grudge against the man accused of attacking him and hoped his heart would be filled with kindness and compassion.
The stabbing comes as the Utah Department of Public Safety says investigators are confronting a significant increase in violent online rhetoric and extremist activity. Tanner Jensen, DPS chief of investigations, said Utah law enforcement agencies investigate more than 100 reported hate crimes each year. He said some of the most common reasons victims are targeted include religion, race, sexual orientation and gender identity. Jensen said hateful or extremist beliefs do not necessarily amount to criminal conduct.
The challenge for investigators is determining when constitutionally protected speech becomes a credible threat or signals that someone may be moving toward violence.
“Right now, it’s more difficult than ever, especially with online and social media and the ubiquitous amounts of threats that we see and knowing where that line is,” Jensen said. Investigators monitor tips, work with local, state and federal partners and assess whether a person appears to be progressing from extremist rhetoric to radicalization and potentially toward action.
“When it comes to online radicalization, online violent rhetoric, it’s a daily occurrence that we have to balance those constitutional rights with possibly some type of criminal investigation,” Jensen said. DPS has seen a substantial increase in violent rhetoric tied to extremist beliefs during the past five to 10 years, according to Jensen.
Law enforcement’s goal is not simply to respond after an attack, he said, but to identify concerning behavior early enough to assess a potential threat and intervene when legally possible.
“The biggest difficulty in catching these crimes is making sure that community members report it to law enforcement,” Jensen said. A tip may not result in an immediate arrest.
However, Jensen said reports can help investigators identify a pattern of conduct, assess a person’s intent, share information among agencies, and determine whether the behavior has crossed into criminal activity. At the town hall, Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill similarly urged Utahns to document and report threats, harassment and suspected bias-motivated crimes.
“I need you not to tolerate this. I need you to report this. I need you to call the police and document this,” Gill said.
“Hate crimes are vehemently underreported. ” Gill said communities should not have to wait until someone is physically harmed before recognizing and confronting intolerance.
“We have to be much better than saying we have to wait till somebody is hurt for us to say there is a problem,” Gill said. Gill said the protections of a free society include not only the ability to express views, but also the ability to challenge intolerance and hatred.
“In a free society, we also get to say what is not appropriate,” Gill said. “In a free society, we also get to question that level of intolerance and hate. And we owe that to each other. ”“You do it because this is what dignity demands on a fundamental level of one person to another,” he said.
Much of Wednesday’s discussion centered on how Muslim Utahns can feel safe following a religiously-motivated attack. Public officials and religious leaders denounced the violence and pledged to remain visible and engaged with the Muslim community. The message repeated throughout the gathering was that preventing hate-motivated violence requires cooperation between law enforcement and the communities most likely to recognize warning signs, before extremist rhetoric escalates into an attack.
